Three traps. English has one command form for everyone ("Speak slowly!"); German has three, depending on who you're talking to — and the du form keeps the vowel change.

Imperativo com «Sie» e com «wir», passo: The imperative with «Sie» and «wir», step by step
O imperativo serve para pedir, dar instr: The imperative is for asking, giving instructions, inviting and telling people what to do. We start with the POLITE form, which you hear in shops, schools and exams. STEP 1: take the infinitive («öffnen») and put «Sie» after it: «Öffnen Sie das Buch.» So the verb comes FIRST and «Sie» right behind it. English drops the "you" in commands; German formal commands keep it. STEP 2: separable verbs: the prefix goes to the END: «Hören Sie zu.», «Stehen Sie auf.» STEP 3: «bitte» makes the request polite and can go in several places: «Öffnen Sie bitte das Buch.» STEP 4: the «wir» form invites people to do something together — the German "let's": «Gehen wir!» (Let's go!), «Fangen wir an!» (Let's begin!). STEP 5: to negate, put «nicht» at the end: «Rauchen Sie nicht!»
o português muda o final do verbo («abra: English commands drop the subject: "Open the book." The German formal imperative keeps it, right after the verb: «Öffnen Sie das Buch» — almost a question without the question mark. And "let's…" is simply the wir form with the verb first: «Gehen wir!»
No imperativo o verbo vem ANTES de «Sie»: In the imperative, the verb comes BEFORE «Sie».
The separable prefix goes to the end.

Imperativo com «du» e «ihr», passo a pas: The imperative with «du» and «ihr», step by step
Com amigos, família e crianças você usa: With friends, family and children you use «du» (one person) or «ihr» (several). STEP 1, «du»: take the du form of the present, drop «du» and the «-st»: «du kommst» → «Komm!» STEP 2: if the verb changes e to i or ie in the present, the imperative KEEPS the change: «du nimmst» → «Nimm!», «du sprichst» → «Sprich!», «du liest» → «Lies!», «du gibst» → «Gib!», «du hilfst» → «Hilf!» STEP 3: if the verb has an umlaut (a → ä), the imperative has NO umlaut: «du fährst» → «Fahr!» STEP 4: a stem in -t or -d adds -e: «Warte!» STEP 5, «ihr»: it's the present form without «ihr»: «Kommt!», «Wartet!» STEP 6: «sein» is irregular: «Sei ruhig!» (du), «Seid ruhig!» (ihr), «Seien Sie ruhig!» (Sie) — compare English "Be quiet!". Separable verbs: «Steh auf!», «Steht auf!»
O imperativo não tem trema (a → ä só no: The imperative has no umlaut (a → ä only in the present).

Learning these phrases now saves you from losing points just because you didn't understand the task. They all follow what you've seen: verb first, «Sie» after, separable prefix at the end.

Com du no presente, sprechen muda e para: With du in the present, sprechen changes e to i: du sprichst. The ending is -st.
Com er no presente, nehmen tem a forma n: With er in the present, nehmen becomes nimmt, with a vowel change and a changed stem: Er nimmt einen Kaffee.
Com wir, usa-se fahren. A mudança a para: With wir, it's fahren. The a → ä change only appears in du fährst and er fährt, not in the plural.
O imperativo de helfen com du é hilf, co: The du imperative of helfen is hilf, with e → i. So: Hilf mir bitte!
No imperativo formal, usa-se o verbo com: In the formal imperative, use the Sie form followed by the pronoun: Sprechen Sie langsam! Sprich is for du.
Com ihr no presente, sprechen fica sprec: With ihr in the present, sprechen is sprecht. The e → i change of du sprichst and er spricht doesn't happen here.
Com du no presente, lesen muda e para ie: With du in the present, lesen changes e to ie: du liest. Lest goes with ihr, not du.

PASSO 1: O erro que mais custa caro é co: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: using one command form for everyone, as in English (Sprich! to your boss, or Sprechen Sie! to your kid); dropping the vowel change in du and er/sie/es (du sprechst, er nehmt); changing the vowel where it doesn't belong (ich fähre); leaving the -st or -t in the du imperative (Gibst / Gibt mir! instead of Gib mir!); and looking for a "don't" — German just adds nicht.
